docs.title: Renal Replacement Therapy and Transplantation
docs.text:
##### Principles (know the two physical processes)

- **Diffusion** — solutes move down a concentration gradient across a semipermeable membrane (clears small solutes: urea, potassium). The basis of **haemodialysis.**
- **Convection / ultrafiltration** — solvent (water) dragged across by a pressure gradient, carrying solutes ("solvent drag"); removes fluid and larger middle molecules. Dominant in **haemofiltration.**
- **Osmosis** — water drawn across by an osmotic gradient (dextrose in dialysate); the basis of fluid removal in **peritoneal dialysis.**

##### Haemodialysis (HD)

- Blood pumped through a dialyser against countercurrent dialysate; usually **3× weekly,**

**~4 hours** in a unit (or home HD).
- **Vascular access — the key exam topic (in order of preference):**
  - **Arteriovenous fistula (AVF)** — **gold standard;** native artery–vein anastomosis; needs **6–8 weeks to "mature";** lowest infection/thrombosis risk, best longevity.

Complications: stenosis/thrombosis, steal syndrome (distal ischaemia), high-output cardiac failure, aneurysm.
  - **AV graft** — synthetic; used when veins inadequate; higher thrombosis/infection than fistula.
  - **Tunnelled central venous catheter** — immediate use but **highest infection** **and thrombosis risk;** last resort/bridge.
  - "Fistula first" — and **never** take blood, cannulate, or put a BP cuff on a fistula arm.
- **Complications: hypotension** (commonest — during fluid removal), cramps, arrhythmia, **dialysis disequilibrium syndrome** (rapid urea/osmolar shifts → cerebral oedema → headache, confusion, seizures — avoided by gentle initial dialysis), access problems, air embolism, anaphylaxis to membrane.

##### Peritoneal dialysis (PD)

- Uses the **peritoneum as the semipermeable membrane;** dialysate instilled via a

Tenckhoff catheter, dextrose osmotic gradient removes fluid. **CAPD** (manual exchanges) or **APD** (overnight machine).
- **Advantages:** home-based, independence, gentler haemodynamics, preserves residual function.
- **Complications:**
  - **PD peritonitis** — the big one: **cloudy effluent + abdominal pain + fever;** diagnose on effluent WCC (>100 with >50% neutrophils) and culture; usually

**Staph** (skin flora); treat with **intraperitoneal antibiotics.**
  - **Exit-site/tunnel infection,** catheter malfunction, hernias, **encapsulating** **peritoneal sclerosis** (rare, serious — bowel encased in fibrous cocoon → obstruction), membrane failure over time, hyperglycaemia/weight gain from glucose load.

##### Choosing a modality & conservative care

- Modality depends on patient factors (comorbidity, lifestyle, home support, residual function, cardiovascular stability), not just clinical criteria — a shared decision.
- **Conservative (supportive) kidney care** is a legitimate pathway for frail/multimorbid patients in whom dialysis may not improve survival or quality of life — focus on symptom control and advance care planning. **Mentioning this shows exam maturity.**

docs.title: Renal Replacement Therapy and Transplantation
docs.text:
The best treatment for ESKD for suitable patients — better survival and quality of life than dialysis.

##### Work-up and matching

- **Living vs deceased donor** (living gives better graft survival, can be pre-emptive before dialysis).
- **Matching: ABO blood group compatibility** and **HLA matching** (HLA-A, -B, -DR most important; DR mismatch matters most). **Crossmatch** (recipient serum against donor lymphocytes) must be negative — a **positive crossmatch predicts hyperacute** **rejection.**
- Placed **extraperitoneally in the iliac fossa,** anastomosed to iliac vessels and bladder; native kidneys usually left in situ.

##### Immunosuppression (and side effects — very examinable)

Typically **triple therapy:**

| Drug class | Example | Key side effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Calcineurin inhibitor | Tacrolimus, ciclosporin | Nephrotoxicity (afferent vasoconstriction — mimics rejection!), tremor, diabetes (tacrolimus), hypertension, gum hypertrophy/hirsutism (ciclosporin), neurotoxicity; narrow therapeutic window → drug-level monitoring |
| Antimetabolite | Mycophenolate mofetil | GI upset, bone marrow suppression, teratogenic |
| Corticosteroid | Prednisolone | Diabetes, osteoporosis, weight gain, infection, cushingoid |
| (mTOR inhibitor) | Sirolimus | Poor wound healing, proteinuria, pneumonitis |
| Induction agent | Basiliximab (IL-2R antibody), ATG | Infusion reactions, infection |

Key trap: **calcineurin inhibitor toxicity can look like rejection** — both cause a rising creatinine in a transplant. Biopsy + drug levels distinguish them.

##### Rejection — types and timing

| Type | Timing | Mechanism | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hyperacute | Minutes–h ours | Pre-formed antibodies (ABO/HLA) | Graft thrombosis; now rare due to crossmatching; untreatable → remove graft |
| Acute cellular | Days–mont hs | T-cell mediated | Commonest acute; treat with high-dose steroids, ATG if severe |
| Acute antibody-medi ated | Days–mont hs | Donor-specific antibodies | Treat with plasma exchange, IVIG, rituximab |
| Chronic | Months–ye ars | Immune + non-immune (interstitial fibrosis/tubular atrophy) | Gradual decline; largely untreatable — leading cause of late graft loss |

##### Long-term complications

- **Infection** (immunosuppression): **CMV** (commonest opportunistic — prophylaxis/monitoring), **BK virus** nephropathy (can mimic rejection), **PJP** (co-trimoxazole prophylaxis), fungal.
- **Malignancy: skin cancers (SCC — very high risk, sun protection essential),** **post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD — EBV-driven).**
- **Cardiovascular disease** — leading cause of death with a functioning graft.
- **Recurrent disease** in the graft (FSGS, IgA, MPGN can recur).
- Drug toxicities, new-onset diabetes after transplant (NODAT), bone disease.

##### Delayed graft function

- Need for dialysis within the first week post-transplant, usually due to **ischaemia-reperfusion ATN** (commoner with deceased/marginal donors and long co

###### Renal Disease Recognition — Formulation

###### & Quick-Spot Summary

A synthesis of the section notes, organised for **pattern recognition:** meet the disease by its presenting syndrome, clinch it with the single differentiating feature. Everything here is cross-checked in the parent section files. Use it as the night-before flick-through.

###### How to use this document

- **Part A** — organised by presenting syndrome (how the patient actually turns up). Find the syndrome, scan the discriminators.
- **Part B** — signature tables: the fastest single-clue lookups (pathognomonic clue, antibody, complement, casts, IF pattern, biochemistry).
- **Part C** — confusable pairs: the head-to-heads students mix up, and the one feature that separates each.

docs.parent: Renal Syndrome Recognition and Lookup Tables
docs.text:
###### First split: pre-renal / intrinsic / post-renal

| Bucket | Points towards it | Clinching feature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-renal | Hypovolaemia, sepsis, HF, cirrhosis, NSAID/ACEi | FeNa <1%, urine osm >500, bland urine, high urea:creatinine; responds to fluid |
| Intrinsic (ATN) | Prolonged pre-renal/toxins/contrast | FeNa >1–2%, urine osm ~300, muddy-brown casts; no response to fluid |
| Post-renal | Older man, single kidney, pelvic malignancy | Hydronephrosis on US; relieved by catheter/nephrostomy |

###### Then the specific AKI syndromes — each has a one-line tell:

| Syndrome | The clue that clinches it |
| --- | --- |
| Rhabdomyolysis | Dipstick blood +++, no RBCs on microscopy; ↑↑CK, ↑K⁺/PO₄³⁻, ↓Ca²⁺ |
| Tumour lysis syndrome | Post-chemo; ↑K⁺, ↑PO₄³⁻, ↑urate, ↓Ca²⁺ ("everything up except calcium") |
| Contrast-associated AKI | Creatinine rises 48–72 h after contrast, recovers |
| Hepatorenal syndrome | Cirrhosis + AKI + urine Na <10 + no response to albumin; bland urine |
| Cholesterol emboli | Post-angiogram + livedo reticularis + eosinophilia + low complement |
| Acute interstitial nephritis | New drug (PPI/NSAID/penicillin) + sterile pyuria + white cell casts ± eosinophilia |
| Scleroderma renal crisis | Systemic sclerosis + severe HTN + AKI + MAHA → give ACE inhibitor |
| Pulmonary–renal syndrome | Haemoptysis + RPGN → anti-GBM or ANCA vasculitis (urgent) |

docs.text:
##### Types and risk factors

| Stone type | ~Frequency | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Calcium oxalate | ~80% (commonest) | Radio-opaque; hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, hypocitraturia; low fluid intake |
| Calcium phosphate |  | Radio-opaque; associated with distal (type 1) RTA, alkaline urine |
| Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) | ~10% | Infection stones (urease-producing organisms — Proteus, Klebsiella); form staghorn calculi; alkaline urine |
| Uric acid | ~5–10% | Radiolucent (won't show on plain film); acidic urine, gout, high purine, tumour lysis |
| Cystine | rare | Inherited cystinuria; hexagonal crystals; from childhood |

##### Presentation and imaging

- **Renal colic:** sudden severe **loin-to-groin pain,** colicky, restless patient (can't get comfortable — contrast with peritonitis where they lie still), nausea, haematuria.
- **Imaging: non-contrast CT KUB is the gold standard** (detects nearly all stones including radiolucent uric acid; ultrasound for pregnancy/children to avoid radiation).

##### Management

- **Analgesia: NSAIDs (e.g. IM/PR diclofenac) are first-line** and superior to opioids for renal colic (caution in AKI/CKD).

- **Most small stones (<5 mm) pass spontaneously; medical expulsive therapy** **(tamsulosin)** may help stones 5–10 mm in the distal ureter.
- **Indications for intervention:** stone unlikely to pass, uncontrolled pain, **obstruction** **with infection (emergency),** AKI, solitary kidney.
- **Modalities: shockwave lithotripsy (ESWL), ureteroscopy + laser, percutaneous** **nephrolithotomy (PCNL)** for large/staghorn stones.
- ⚠ **Obstructed + infected kidney = urological emergency** → **urgent decompression** (nephrostomy or ureteric stent) + antibiotics. Do not delay for stone removal.
- **Prevention:** high fluid intake (>2.5 L/day), reduce salt/animal protein, normal dietary calcium (not low), thiazides for hypercalciuria, potassium citrate, allopurinol for uric acid.

| Pyelonephritis | Fever, rigors, loin pain, nausea/vomiting + LUTS; white cell casts | Broader/longer antibiotics; admit if unwell; image if not improving |

docs.text:
- **Causes:** luminal (stone, clot), mural (stricture, tumour), extrinsic **(BPH/prostate cancer**

— commonest in older men, pelvic malignancy, retroperitoneal fibrosis, AAA).
- **Hydronephrosis** on ultrasound (may be absent early or if ureters encased).
- **Post-obstructive diuresis:** after relieving chronic bilateral obstruction, a **massive** **diuresis** can follow (accumulated solute/urea, tubular dysfunction, volume overload correction) → **monitor fluid balance and electrolytes closely,** replace losses.
- **Benign prostatic hyperplasia:** LUTS (hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia, incomplete emptying); can cause **chronic retention → obstructive AKI.** Treat with **α-blockers** **(tamsulosin)** ± **5α-reductase inhibitors (finasteride);** catheterise acute retention.

docs.title: Structural and Urological Renal Disease
docs.text:
##### Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)

- **Genetics: PKD1 (chromosome 16, ~85%, more severe)** or **PKD2 (chromosome 4,** **milder);** autosomal dominant.
- **Renal:** bilateral enlarging cysts → **hypertension** (early), haematuria, cyst infection/haemorrhage, stones, progressive CKD → ESKD.
- **Extra-renal manifestations (examinable): berry (intracranial) aneurysms →** **subarachnoid haemorrhage, hepatic cysts,** mitral valve prolapse, **diverticular** **disease,** abdominal wall hernias.
- **Management:** BP control **(ACEi/ARB),** treat complications; **tolvaptan (V2 receptor** **antagonist)** ⚑ slows cyst growth and eGFR decline in rapidly progressing ADPKD — a relatively recent disease-modifying option (monitor LFTs, causes marked aquaresis/thirst). Screen family; consider MRA screening for aneurysms if family history.

##### Other cystic disease

- **Simple cysts** — very common, benign, incidental; use the **Bosniak classification** to grade malignant potential of complex cysts.
- **Acquired cystic disease** — in long-standing dialysis patients; increased RCC risk.
- **Medullary sponge kidney** — cystic dilatation of collecting ducts; recurrent stones and infection, usually benign.
- (Autosomal recessive PKD — infantile, rarer, severe.)

docs.title: Structural and Urological Renal Disease
docs.text:
##### Renal cell carcinoma (RCC)

- Arises from **proximal tubular epithelium; clear cell** commonest. Risk: smoking, obesity, **VHL disease,** dialysis-acquired cysts.
- **Classic triad (haematuria + loin pain + flank mass)** is late and uncommon (<10%); most found incidentally on imaging.
- **Paraneoplastic syndromes (a favourite): polycythaemia (EPO), hypercalcaemia**

###### (PTHrP), hypertension (renin), Stauffer syndrome (non-metastatic hepatic

**dysfunction).**
- **Spread:** into **renal vein/IVC** (can cause a **left varicocele** if it obstructs the left gonadal vein), lungs ("cannonball" metastases).
- Management: **surgery (partial/radical nephrectomy);** tyrosine kinase inhibitors/immunotherapy for advanced disease (relatively chemo/radio-resistant).

##### Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma

- Bladder/ureter/renal pelvis; **painless visible haematuria;** risk: **smoking, aromatic** **amines (dye/rubber industry),** cyclophosphamide.
- Diagnosis: **cystoscopy + CT urogram + urine cytology.**

##### Prostate cancer (renal relevance)

- Can cause **bladder outflow / ureteric obstruction → post-renal AKI.** Presents with

LUTS, bone pain (sclerotic mets), raised PSA.

##### Haematuria — the diagnostic pathway

- **Visible (macroscopic) haematuria** → always investigate: **cystoscopy + upper-tract** **imaging (CT urogram),** especially **painless visible haematuria in an older smoker =** **malignancy until excluded.**
- **Non-visible (microscopic):** confirm it's real (not myoglobin/haemoglobin — check microscopy for RBCs), exclude UTI, then assess with imaging/cystoscopy if persistent or with risk factors.
- **Glomerular vs urological bleeding: dysmorphic RBCs, red cell casts, proteinuria**

**→ glomerular (nephrology); isomorphic RBCs, clots, no casts → urological** **(urology).**

docs.text:
- POTTER SYNDROME: in bilateral renal agenesis or obstructive uropathy (Pulmonary hypoplasia, Oligohydramnios – trigger, Twisted face, Twisted skin, Extremity defects, Renal failure- in utero)

- HORSESHOE KIDNEY: inferior kidney poles fuse and the ureters course medially and anteriorly over joined renal isthmus  can cause hydronephrosis, uteropelvic joint obstruction, renal stones, infection, chromosomal aneuploidy syndromes (Turner syndrome, trisomies 13/18/21), renal cancer

- CONGENITAL SOLITARY FUNCTIONING KIDNEY: one functioning kidney; majority asymptomatic

- UNILATERAL RENAL AGENESIS: complete absence of kidney/ureter

- MULTICYSTIC DYSPLASTIC KIDNEY: non-functional kidney with cysts + connective tissue (bilateral=POTTER)

- DUPLEX COLLECTING SYSTEM: associated with vesicoureteral reflux and/or ureteral obstruction,  risk for UTIs

- POSTERIOR URETHRAL VALVES:  urethral obstruction and bladder outlet obstruction in male infants, and can be diagnosed prenatally by hydronephrosis and dilated/thick-walled bladder on U/S

- RENAL ECTOPIA: Abnormal renal location usually results when a kidney fails to ascend from its origin in the true pelvis. It can cause ureteropelvic junction obstruction, vesicoureteral reflux and multicystic renal dysplasia

- RENAL HYPOPLASIA:  ureteral bud branching; underdeveloped kidney with histologically normal nephrons

- VESICOURETERAL REFLUX DISEASE: most common congenital abnormality and is discovered in utero through a morphology scan at 18 weeks. High grades are associated with renal failure and sclerotic renal lesions.

- 70% glandular and 30% stromal tissue

- Secretes fluid that nourishes and protects sperm – alkaline to neutralize vaginal acidity, proteolytic enzymes, prostatic acid phosphatase, PSA

Cross-checked against Robbins, StatPearls, and standard renal physiology/clinical texts. The

docs.title: Tubulointerstitial and Tubular Disorders
docs.text:
##### Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN)

- **Mechanism:** hypersensitivity reaction causing inflammation of the renal interstitium →

AKI.
- **Causes:**
  - **Drugs (~70%): NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors, penicillins/cephalosporins,**

###### allopurinol, rifampicin, sulfonamides, diuretics

  - **Infection:** pyelonephritis, leptospirosis, legionella
  - **Autoimmune/systemic:** sarcoidosis, Sjögren's, SLE, **TINU** (tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis)
- **Classic triad** (fever, rash, eosinophilia) — present in **<10%,** so its absence doesn't exclude AIN.
- **Investigations:** AKI, **sterile pyuria, white cell casts, eosinophiluria** (poor sensitivity/specificity — no longer relied upon), mild proteinuria.
- **Management: stop the offending drug** (the key step); **corticosteroids** if no improvement or severe. Usually recovers, but can leave chronic damage.

##### Chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis

- Slowly progressive interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy.
- **Analgesic nephropathy:** chronic heavy use (esp. old compound analgesics with phenacetin); **papillary necrosis;** look for a "ring sign" on imaging.
- **Lithium nephrotoxicity: nephrogenic diabetes insipidus** (commonest renal effect) and chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis; monitor levels and renal function.
- Others: chronic obstruction/reflux, sarcoidosis, heavy metals, aristolochic acid, myeloma.

docs.title: Tubulointerstitial and Tubular Disorders
docs.text:
All RTAs cause a **normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis.** Distinguish by potassium, urine pH, and associated features. Normal anion gap = bicarb loss w/ compensatory hyperchloraemic; vs high anion gap = increased acids added e.g. ketoacid, lactic acid, toxins

|  | Type 1 (Distal) | Type 2 (Proximal) | Type 4 (Hyperkalaemic) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Defect | Distal H⁺ secretion fails (α-intercalated cell) | Proximal HCO₃⁻ reabsorption fails | Aldosterone deficiency/resistance |
| Serum K⁺ | LOW (hypokalaemia) | LOW (hypokalaemia) | HIGH (hyperkalaemia) |
| Urine pH | >5.5 (inappropriately high) — can't acidify urine | Variable; <5.5 once below reabsorptive threshold | <5.5 (appropriately low) |
| Causes | Autoimmune (Sjögren's, RA), hypercalciuria, amphotericin, genetic | Fanconi syndrome, myeloma, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, Wilson's, cystinosis | Diabetes (commonest), Addison's, ACEi/ARB, NSAIDs, heparin, trimethoprim, spironolactone |
| Complication s | Nephrocalcinosis, calcium phosphate stones (alkaline urine, hypercalciuria, hypocitraturia); rickets/osteomalacia | Rickets/osteomalacia; stones uncommon | Mild acidosis |
| Treatment | Oral bicarbonate/citrate; potassium replacement | Bicarbonate (large doses needed) + potassium; thiazide | Fludrocortisone, dietary K⁺ restriction, loop diuretic; stop offending drugs |

**The urine anion gap** (Na⁺ + K⁺ − Cl⁻) — used to work out the cause of a normal-anion-gap acidosis:
- **Negative** ("neg-GUT-ive") → **GI bicarbonate loss (diarrhoea)** — kidney appropriately excreting NH₄Cl
- **Positive** → **RTA** — kidney failing to excrete ammonium

Memory hooks: Type **1** = **one** = distal = high urine pH + stones. Type **2** = proximal = Fanconi.

Type **4** = the only **hyperkalaemic** RTA = **hypoaldosteronism.**

docs.text:
- **Generalised proximal tubular dysfunction** → failure to reabsorb multiple solutes:
  - **Glycosuria (with normal blood glucose),** aminoaciduria, phosphaturia (→ hypophosphataemia → **osteomalacia/rickets),** bicarbonaturia (→ **type 2 RTA),** uricosuria, tubular proteinuria, **hypokalaemia**
- **Causes: myeloma (commonest acquired cause in adults),** drugs **(tenofovir,** ifosfamide, aminoglycosides, expired tetracyclines), heavy metals, **Wilson's disease,** **cystinosis** (commonest inherited, children), Sjögren's.
- Recognise it from the combination: glycosuria + normoglycaemia + hypophosphataemia

+ hypokalaemia + acidosis.

docs.text:
| Disorder | "Acts like" | Defect | Key electrolytes | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bartter syndrome | Loop diuretic (furosemide) | NKCC2 in thick ascending limb | Hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, normal/low BP, hypercalciuria | Presents younger/more severe; normal Mg²⁺; may have nephrocalcinosis |
| Gitelman syndrome | Thiazide | NCC in distal convoluted tubule | Hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, normal/low BP, HYPOcalciuria | Hypomagnesaemia ; milder, older presentation |
| Liddle syndrome | Excess ENaC activity ("always-on" aldosterone effect) | Gain-of-fun ction ENaC | Hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, HYPERTENSION, LOW renin & aldosterone | Treat with amiloride (not spironolactone) |
| Apparent mineralocorticoi d excess | Cortisol acting on MR | 11β-HSD2 deficiency (can't inactivate cortisol) | Hypokalaemia, alkalosis, hypertension, low renin/aldosterone | Also caused by liquorice excess |

###### Discriminators worth locking in:

- **Bartter vs Gitelman:** both look like diuretic abuse (hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, normal/low BP), but **calcium separates them — Bartter = hyperCALCiuria (loop-like),**

###### Gitelman = hypoCALCiuria + hypomagnesaemia (thiazide-like).

- **Liddle vs Bartter/Gitelman:** Liddle is **HYPERtensive with LOW aldosterone** — it mimics hyperaldosteronism but the aldosterone is suppressed, and it responds to **amiloride, not spironolactone.**

##### Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus

- **Collecting duct resistance to ADH** → inability to concentrate urine → **polyuria,** **polydipsia, dilute urine despite raised plasma osmolality.**
- **Causes: lithium** (commonest acquired), **hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia,** chronic kidney disease, inherited **(AVPR2** X-linked, or aquaporin-2).
- **Water deprivation test:** urine stays dilute after deprivation AND **fails to concentrate** **after desmopressin** (distinguishes from cranial DI, which does respond to desmopressin).
- **Management:** treat the cause; **thiazides (paradoxical antidiuresis),** **low-salt/low-protein diet, amiloride** (esp. lithium-induced).

Acute/chronic inflammation of the renal tubules and interstitium

##### acute tubulo-interstitial nephritis

| Definition | Rapid (days to weeks) decline in renal function and accounts for 10-20% of all AKI |
|---|---|
| Aetiology | Hypersensitivity: antibiotics (B-lactams, sulphonamides, rifampin, quinolones, cephalosporins), NSAIDs, diuretics, allopurinol, PPIs, phenytoin, acyclovir, methotrexate Infectious: bacterial pyelonephritis, leptospirosis, streptococcus, legionella, CMV, EBV Immune: SLE, Sjogren’s, sarcoidosis Idiopathic Note: Pee (diuretics) Pain (NSAIDs) Penicillins and cephalosporins Proton pump inhibitors RifamPicin |
| Pathophysiology | Hypersensitivity or tubular obstruction/toxicity  inflammatory cells infiltrate interstitium |
| Presentation | Underlying disease symptoms AKI: painless haematuria Hypersensitivity: fever, rash, arthralgia Pyelonephritis: CVA tenderness, flank pain |
| Investigations | Urine: proteinuria, haematuria, pyuria, WBC casts, eosinophils (AIN) Bloods:  urea,  Cr, eosinophilia (drug reaction), metabolic acidosis (RTA), PO43-, K+, Na+ Renal biopsy definite Gallium scan:  signal=infiltrate |
| Management | Discontinue drugs and IVF Antibiotics if infectious Corticosteroids in allergic or immune disease |
| Prognosis | Recovery within 2 weeks if insult can be eliminated |

##### chronic tubulo-interstitial nephritis

| Definition | Slowly progressive renal failure, moderate proteinuria and abnormal tubular function signs |
|---|---|
| Aetiology | Persistent acute TIN UTI/chronic pyelonephritis: tumours, stones, bladder outlet obstruction, VUR Nephrotoxins Analgesic nephropathy: NSAIDs, acetaminophen Crystal-induced: acyclovir, methotrexate, cisplatin, lithium, cyclosporine Heavy metals Vascular disease Malignancies: multiple myeloma, lymphoma Immune: SLE, Sjogren’s, anti-GBM, sarcoidosis Hereditary: cystic disease, sickle cell disease |
| Pathophysiology | prostacyclin synthesis → vasoconstriction of the medullary blood vessels → papillary ischemia/necrosis, fibrosis of interstitium with tubular atrophy, mononuclear cell inflammation |
| Presentation | Painless haematuria, pyuria, fatigue, nausea Underlying aetiology- colicky pain due to papillary necrosis, multiple myeloma Renal papillary necrosis: coagulative necrosis of the renal medullary pyramids and papillae Aetiology (POSTCARDS): pyelonephritis, obstruction, sickle cell disease, Tb, cirrhosis, analgesia, renal transplant rejection, DM, systemic vasculitis Ischemia  necrosis and sloughing of the papillae  ureteral obstruction  scarring |
| Investigations | Tubular dysfunction: e.g. acidosis, electrolyte disturbances e.g. K+ Progressive renal failure: azotemia, uremia Ultrasound: shrunken kidneys with irregular contours |
| Management | Stop offending agent or treat underlying disease Supportive measures: correct metabolic disorders (Ca2+, PO43- and anaemia) Forced diuresis If necessary, plasmapheresis/dialysis |
